opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's really a natural continuation, because security has always been about one question: who has power in a system, and how do you protect the people with less of it?

For much of my career, that meant looking at networks, mobile systems, and online platforms, and asking how attackers could exploit them and how we could defend against that. Over time I found myself drawn to the adversarial side of machine learning: how models can be fooled, poisoned, or manipulated. For a long time that was framed as a threat, something attackers do to models.

What changed for me was realizing that the dynamics had flipped in some cases. With generative AI, the people being harmed often aren't the companies running the models. They're individuals: artists whose work gets scraped and mimicked without consent, people whose faces end up in recognition systems they never agreed to. These people have very little leverage. They can't sue every company or opt out of systems that don't respect opt-outs.

So the question became: can we take the same adversarial techniques we used to study as attacks and turn them into tools that give individuals some agency back? That's the thread through projects like Fawkes for facial recognition, and later Glaze and Nightshade for artists. The core techniques are things the security and ML communities have understood for years: perturbations, poisoning, exploiting the gap between how humans and models perceive things. We're just pointing them in a different direction, toward protecting the person rather than the system.

The security mindset also keeps us honest. You never assume a defense is permanent. You expect countermeasures, you think about adaptive attackers, you try to raise costs rather than promise perfection. That's how we approach this work. We're not claiming to solve the problem forever. We're trying to shift the economics so that respecting people's work and consent becomes the easier path than ignoring it.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's funny, because from the outside it probably looks like a hard pivot. For most of my career I was doing fairly traditional systems and security work, things like network security, bots, detecting fake accounts and Sybil attacks in social networks, side channels, that kind of thing. And then around 2017, 2018, I started looking at adversarial machine learning, and people assumed I'd just jumped on the deep learning bandwagon.

But to me it's really the same problem viewed from a different angle. Security research is fundamentally about asymmetry. You've got an attacker with some set of capabilities, you've got a defender who usually has fewer resources, and you're trying to figure out where the real leverage is. What's changed is who the attacker is and who the defender is. Ten years ago I was thinking about how to protect a service like Facebook or a bank from people abusing it. Now, with things like Fawkes, and then Glaze and Nightshade, the people we're trying to protect are individuals, ordinary users, artists, who are on the receiving end of very large, very well-funded systems. The power imbalance is just enormous.

And the techniques carry over more than you'd expect. When we were working on Fawkes, which cloaks photos so facial recognition models can't learn your face properly, that's really a poisoning attack dressed up as a defense. The attacker's model is unauthorized facial recognition, and we're the ones injecting noise into its training pipeline. Glaze is the same intuition applied to style mimicry in generative image models. Nightshade takes it a step further and actually tries to impose a cost on scraping without consent. So all of the adversarial ML work we did early on, understanding how models fail, how brittle they are, how you can manipulate what they learn, that became the toolbox for building protections.

The other thing that's a straight continuation is the mindset. Security people are constitutionally skeptical. You don't trust the system to be benevolent, you don't assume the policy will be followed, you assume someone will push on every seam. I think that's actually been missing in a lot of the AI conversation, where the default assumption is that the technology is good and the misuse is an edge case. From where I sit, after twenty-some years of watching people abuse every system that was ever deployed at scale, misuse isn't the edge case. It's the baseline you have to design for. So in that sense, I don't think I changed fields at all. The field came to me.

astra-6.text:
I see it as a pretty natural continuation. In security, you’re always asking: who has power in a system, how could that power be abused, and what can we do to protect the people on the receiving end? AI changes the technology, but those questions are still very much the same.

The important shift is that the people affected may have very little control over the system. They didn’t build the model, they may not have agreed to participate, and yet its use can affect their work or their lives. So the research question becomes: can we give those people some practical way to defend themselves?

That’s the connection for me. It’s not simply about finding a vulnerability or making an algorithm more robust. It’s about understanding an adversarial situation and building something that gives people more agency.

sol-6.1.text:
I see it as a continuation of the same basic question: when a technology becomes widely available, how can someone abuse it, and how do we protect the people affected? In security, you’re always thinking about the adversary—what they want, what capabilities they have, and where existing defenses fall short.

AI introduces new capabilities, but that way of thinking still applies. We’re asking who bears the cost when these systems are misused, and whether we can give those people practical ways to protect themselves. For me, the connection is that the technology is the subject of the research, but protecting people is the purpose.
